theme: Why the work exists: need, value and the people concerned
definition: A gap, problem or opportunity in an organization's situation that is serious enough to justify effort on a change.

theme: Why the work exists: need, value and the people concerned
definition: The benefit, in terms the organization itself cares about, that a change is expected to bring and against which it is judged afterwards.
practice_areas: Business analysis; Transition, deployment and release

theme: Why the work exists: need, value and the people concerned
definition: Any person, group or system whose interests are touched by the work or its result, or who can influence either.

theme: Why the work exists: need, value and the people concerned
definition: Something a stakeholder cares about that the result must respect, recorded before it has been turned into any requirement.

theme: Why the work exists: need, value and the people concerned
definition: The part of the organization and its environment in which a change will happen; it limits what an analysis has to take into account.

theme: Why the work exists: need, value and the people concerned
definition: One candidate way of meeting a need, kept beside the others until a choice has been made and its reasons recorded.

theme: Why the work exists: need, value and the people concerned
definition: A belief taken as true for the purposes of the work without having been confirmed, which must be revisited if it turns out false.

theme: Why the work exists: need, value and the people concerned
definition: A limit on the solution or the work, set by someone with authority or by the environment, that is not open to negotiation within the effort.

theme: Why the work exists: need, value and the people concerned
definition: The pair of descriptions, how the organization works now and how it is meant to work after the change, whose difference defines the change.

theme: Why the work exists: need, value and the people concerned
definition: A sequenced view of the abilities an organization intends to gain, used to place single changes in a larger direction and to see which change enables which.

theme: Knowing the field: domain knowledge and its limits
definition: The field of activity whose concepts, rules and vocabulary are shared by a family of systems.

theme: Knowing the field: domain knowledge and its limits
definition: The agreed terms of a field and their meanings, kept so that models, requirements and conversations about the field do not drift apart.

theme: Knowing the field: domain knowledge and its limits
definition: A statement that constrains or derives something in how an organization operates, held independently of the software that will enforce it.

theme: Knowing the field: domain knowledge and its limits
definition: A representation of the concepts of a field and how they relate, independent of any one product built in it.

theme: Knowing the field: domain knowledge and its limits
definition: The line that decides which concerns belong to the shared assets of a field and which are left to individual products.

theme: Knowing the field: domain knowledge and its limits
definition: The deliberate work of drawing out what experienced people know implicitly and recording it so others can use and check it.

theme: Knowing the field: domain knowledge and its limits
definition: A statement of how an organization carries out a sequence of work to reach a result, used to find where a change is needed.

theme: Knowing the field: domain knowledge and its limits
definition: The organization of the things an enterprise needs to remember about, with their attributes and relationships, described apart from storage technology.
practice_areas: Business analysis; Domain engineering; Technical (system) analysis

theme: Sameness and difference: commonality and variability
definition: What every member of a family of products has in common, and which can therefore be built once.

theme: Sameness and difference: commonality and variability
definition: The decision about which products a family is meant to cover and which it deliberately leaves out.

theme: Sameness and difference: commonality and variability
definition: A characteristic of a product that matters to a stakeholder and that tells products of a family apart; the unit in which choices are discussed.
practice_areas: Application engineering (product line); Business analysis; Domain engineering

theme: Sameness and difference: commonality and variability
definition: A place in a shared asset where members of the family differ and a choice has to be made.

theme: Sameness and difference: commonality and variability
definition: One of the ways in which a variation point can be resolved.

theme: Sameness and difference: commonality and variability
definition: The moment in the life of a product at which a choice at a variation point becomes fixed, from design to run time.
practice_areas: Application engineering (product line); Domain engineering; Integration and build

theme: Sameness and difference: commonality and variability
definition: A rule that forbids or demands certain combinations of choices, so that only workable products can be specified.

theme: Sameness and difference: commonality and variability
definition: The way a variation point is made to work inside an asset, for example by parameters, substitution, extension or selection.

theme: Sameness and difference: commonality and variability
definition: An explicit description of the variation points, alternatives and constraints of a family, used to guide and check configuration.

theme: Sameness and difference: commonality and variability
definition: The deliberate making of a product different from its siblings in a way that stakeholders can notice.

theme: Reusable assets and how they live
definition: Any work product built so that more than one product can use it, whether a requirement, a model, a component or a test.

theme: Reusable assets and how they live
definition: What is known about an asset's origin, quality evidence and intended context, so that someone can judge whether it suits a new use.

theme: Reusable assets and how they live
definition: Choosing, from the available assets, those that meet the needs of a particular product.

theme: Reusable assets and how they live
definition: Changing a selected asset, within what its variation points allow, so that it fits the product at hand.

theme: Reusable assets and how they live
definition: Change to a reusable asset over time, together with its effect on the products that already depend on it.

theme: Reusable assets and how they live
definition: The organized, searchable listing of assets with enough description to find and compare them.

theme: Reusable assets and how they live
definition: Information that flows from product work back to the shared assets: defects found, options missing, uses that were not foreseen.

theme: Reusable assets and how they live
definition: The extra up-front effort spent making something general, justified only by the use it is expected to get in several products.
The complete set of choices that defines one product of a family.
The work of producing a specific product from shared assets according to a configuration.
The part of a product's needs that the shared assets do not cover and which therefore needs product-specific work.
Work done for one product only, beyond what the shared assets offer, kept separate so it does not erode them.
Verification, before building, that a configuration respects all constraints of the variability model.
The record of which assets and choices went into which product, so that later changes can be traced to the products they affect.
practice_areas: Application engineering (product line); Integration and build

definition: A need of one customer that the family does not yet address and that may be absorbed into the shared assets or kept apart.
An expression, in the stakeholder's own terms, of something they want to achieve.
A condition or capability that a solution must have, worded so that it can be agreed and checked.
The set of qualities that make a requirement usable, such as being clear, single-minded, feasible and checkable.
The person, document or situation from which a requirement comes, kept so that it can be questioned and defended.
A situation in which two requirements cannot both be satisfied as written, calling for negotiation or a decision.
The observable condition under which a stakeholder will agree that a requirement has been met.
practice_areas: Business analysis; Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

definition: A modification to an agreed requirement, assessed for its effects before it is accepted.
The relative importance given to a requirement, with the reasons, used when not everything can be done.
A property such as speed, safety or usability that describes how well a solution behaves rather than what it does.
The agreed set of requirements at a point in time, against which later changes are measured.
A decision that has to be made, framed so that evidence can answer it.
A situation in which improving one desirable property costs another, requiring a reasoned balance.
An assessment of whether a proposed solution can be achieved within the limits of technology, time, cost and organization.
A reasoned expectation of an uncertain quantity such as effort, cost or performance, stated with its basis and its uncertainty.
The possibility that uncertainty will affect an objective, described by what could happen, how likely it is and how much it would matter.
How much a result changes when an assumption or input changes, used to see which uncertainties matter.
The recorded reasons that connect evidence to a decision, so that it can be reviewed or reopened.
The structured weighing of alternatives against agreed criteria.
A deliberately simplified description of something, made for a purpose and judged by how well it serves that purpose.
The reason a model is made, which decides what it must show and what it may leave out.
The degree of detail a model carries, chosen to suit its purpose and its readers.
A particular way of looking at a system that brings some concerns to the front and sets others aside.
The absence of contradiction between the parts or views of a model, or between a model and the things it refers to.
The degree to which a model gives answers that hold for the real situation it stands for.
A depiction of the parts of a system and how they are related.
A depiction of how a system acts over time or in response to stimuli.
The use of a model as the agreed reference from which other work products are produced or checked.
A model that states what a thing is, how it is arranged and how its parts relate, without computing anything about it.
A model that can be evaluated to give numbers or verdicts about a property of the thing, such as load, delay, cost or failure likelihood.
A model kept in the notation and tools of one engineering discipline, which must be related to the whole-system model without being absorbed by it.
The agreed way in which information moves between the whole-system model and a discipline model, so that a change on one side can be seen and absorbed on the other.
Running a model, with prepared data and a prepared environment, to observe behaviour that cannot be reached by inspection, and judging the results against what is expected.
Holding the criteria, the evaluated alternatives and the reasons for the choice in or next to the model, so that a decision can be reproduced and challenged later.
Checking a design or a product against its requirements by means of models, so that the checks can be prepared early and repeated when the design changes.
practice_areas: Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

definition: The managed store in which models, their patterns and their versions are kept so that they can be found, compared and reused.
A recurring, proven way of building a part of a model, together with the rule that says what it may and may not be used for.
Treating a change to a model like a change to any other controlled item: identified, assessed, approved and recorded against the version it alters.
An agreement on who may author, change and share which part of a model, and on how consistency is kept while several people work on it.
The chosen combination of purpose, method, notation, tools and flow of work by which an organization models, written down so that it can be deployed and improved.
A stated reason for modelling together with a way to tell whether the modelling is delivering it.
Anything that makes modelling possible and can be reused, such as a library, a template, a method or a tool extension, managed with its own life cycle.
Keeping the ways of working and the tool customizations that proved useful as shared knowledge, instead of letting each team rebuild them.
The climb from raw engineering data, to organized information, to knowledge about the system, to judgement about what to do; a model is useful when it supports each step.
A deliberately chosen set of parts brought together at one time, small enough that a failure can be traced.
The shared statement of what one part offers and another may rely on, so they can be built apart and still fit.
The planned sequence in which parts are combined, chosen to find risky mismatches early.
The transformation of sources and dependencies into runnable artifacts by a defined, repeatable procedure.
A build that gives the same result from the same inputs, wherever and whenever it is run.
A part that another part needs in order to be built or to run, whether made in-house or obtained elsewhere.
A product of a build, such as a package or image, that is stored and can be tested or deployed.
practice_areas: Integration and build; Transition, deployment and release

definition: The unambiguous naming and version of an artifact, so that what was tested is what is released.
practice_areas: Integration and build; Transition, deployment and release

definition: A defect in which two parts that each work alone fail together because they hold different understandings of their boundary.
The closeness of the environments in which software is built, tested and run, which limits surprises when it moves between them.
practice_areas: Integration and build; Transition, deployment and release

definition: A named, fixed state of the sources from which a build can always be produced again.
The decision on how and in what sequence parts will be combined, chosen to expose interface problems early and to isolate the cause of a fault.
The tools, services and test surroundings that must exist before parts can be combined and checked, planned and obtained like any other need.
A simulator, stub or prototype used in place of a part that does not yet exist or cannot be reached, so that the rest can be combined and checked.
The rule for which earlier checks are repeated when a part changes, so that a new combination does not silently break an old one.
practice_areas: Integration and build; Transition, deployment and release

definition: A limit found while combining parts that must be passed back to requirements, architecture and design, because only the design can remove it.
An unexpected result observed while combining parts, recorded with its context so that it can be traced to a cause and not rediscovered.
An ordered, automated sequence of stages that carries a change from source toward a deliverable and records what happened.
practice_areas: Integration and build; Transition, deployment and release

definition: A point in a pipeline at which a change must meet stated conditions before it moves on.
practice_areas: Integration and build; Transition, deployment and release

definition: Keeping the description of a pipeline in versioned, reviewable files like any other source.
The delay between making a change and learning whether it broke anything; the shorter it is, the cheaper a mistake.
The habit of merging small changes into a shared line of work often, with automatic checks on each.
The discipline of keeping the main line of work in a condition from which a release could be made at any time.
practice_areas: Integration and build; Transition, deployment and release

definition: The practice of releasing every change that passes its checks without a separate manual step.
Assurance that the inputs, tools and steps that produce an artifact have not been altered or substituted.
practice_areas: Integration and build; Transition, deployment and release

definition: The ability to see what a pipeline did and why, from its records, without re-running it.
practice_areas: Integration and build; Transition, deployment and release

definition: Working practice in which those who build and those who run software share responsibility for its whole life.
practice_areas: Integration and build; Transition, deployment and release

definition: A version proposed for release, frozen so that the evidence gathered about it applies to what is released.
The state in which stated conditions for releasing, such as evidence, approvals and preparedness, have been met.
The placing of software into an environment where it will run and making it ready to do so.
The way a release reaches its users, for example all at once, in stages or to a small group first, chosen to limit harm.
The prepared means of returning to a known good state if a release goes wrong.
The point at which work moves from the old way of working, or the old system, to the new one.
The movement and conversion of existing data into the form the new system needs, with checks that nothing is lost or changed.
The preparedness of the people who will use and run the result, through training, guidance and support.
The record of what was released, when, to where, on what evidence and by whose decision.
The transfer of responsibility for a running result from those who built it to those who will run it, with what they need to do so.
The stakeholder's confirmation that the result meets what was agreed and may be taken into use.
practice_areas: Business analysis; Transition, deployment and release

definition: Observation after release to confirm that the result behaves as intended in real use.
The plan for moving a product into use: the kind of move, how success is judged, how often it recurs, how disruption and risk are limited and what is done if it fails.
Making the place the product will run in ready for it: sites, networks, enabling services and the people who will operate it.
practice_areas: Integration and build; Transition, deployment and release

definition: A release made outside the normal rhythm to remove a harmful fault or a security weakness, with a lighter path that still leaves a record.
The prepared way back to the last working state when a move into use fails, tested before it is needed.
A limit on how a product can be moved into use that must be given back to requirements, architecture and design, because the design decides it.
practice_areas: Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

definition: An unexpected result observed while moving a product into use, recorded so that the next move starts from it.
The reasoned decision to stop providing a product, a variant or a capability, with who decided and why.
The prepared sequence of steps, owners and dates by which something is withdrawn.
The decision and action for each body of data at retirement: keep, move, archive or destroy, within legal and contractual duties.
Finding and resolving everything that relies on the thing being retired, so that its removal does not break others.
Keeping what is worth knowing about a retired product, such as decisions, designs and lessons, in a form others can find.
Safe removal of the infrastructure, access and configuration that served a retired product.
A duty that outlives a product, such as legal retention, support commitments or warranty.
Moving users and data from a retired product to its replacement, if there is one.
The retirement of one variant of a family while the family and its other variants continue.
A limit on how a product may be ended, such as data ownership, legal retention or security, that must be given to requirements, architecture and design while the product is still being made.
A tool, facility or service needed only to end the product, such as an archive or a secure erasure service, planned and checked before the ending begins.
Telling everyone who depends on the product, in good time, what will end, when, and what replaces it.
The ways an element can leave service: reuse elsewhere, archiving, reconditioning, recycling or destruction, chosen by the value it still has and the risk of keeping it.
Making sure that what was retired cannot return to use by accident, for example by removing keys, licences, access and copies.
Retiring only the elements affected by a change while the rest continues in use, which needs the boundary between them to be known.
A recorded observation or result that supports a claim about the work or the product.

definition: Confirmation, by examination or test, that a work product meets what was specified for it.
practice_areas: Integration and build; Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

definition: Confirmation that a result fulfils its intended use in its real or realistic setting, which may differ from what was specified.
practice_areas: Business analysis; Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

definition: The ability to follow a link from one work product to those it came from or led to, in both directions.
practice_areas: Application engineering (product line); Business analysis; Disposal; Domain engineering; Integration and build; Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

definition: A structured argument, backed by evidence, that a stated property such as safety or security holds.
practice_areas: Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

definition: A note of a significant decision with its context, alternatives considered and reasons.
practice_areas: Application engineering (product line); Business analysis; Disposal; Domain engineering; Integration and build; Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

definition: A checkpoint with explicit criteria that must be met before work continues or is accepted.
practice_areas: Integration and build; Transition, deployment and release

definition: Examination of a work product by people other than its author in order to find problems and improve it.
practice_areas: Application engineering (product line); Business analysis; Disposal; Domain engineering; Integration and build; Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

definition: Adapting a general way of working to the needs, size and risks of a particular project or product.
practice_areas: Application engineering (product line); Business analysis; Disposal; Domain engineering; Integration and build; Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

definition: The chosen way of carrying out a piece of work, including methods, roles and amount of ceremony.
practice_areas: Business analysis; Domain engineering; Technical (system) analysis

definition: The rules for how analysis results are stored, shared, changed and kept.
A recorded result of work with a stated purpose, audience and content, as opposed to the activity that produced it.
practice_areas: Application engineering (product line); Business analysis; Disposal; Domain engineering; Integration and build; Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

definition: A description of the stages a product passes through from first idea to withdrawal, used to plan and govern the work.
practice_areas: Application engineering (product line); Business analysis; Disposal; Domain engineering; Integration and build; Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

definition: A defined set of responsibilities together with the abilities needed to carry them out.
practice_areas: Application engineering (product line); Business analysis; Disposal; Domain engineering; Integration and build; Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

definition: The deliberate use of what was learned to change how the work is done next time.
The planned involvement of stakeholders in the work, matched to their interest and influence.
A task carried out wholly or partly by an artificial agent, whose output is treated as a proposal until a responsible person or check accepts it.
practice_areas: Application engineering (product line); Business analysis; Disposal; Domain engineering; Integration and build; Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

definition: A place in the work at which a person, not an agent, must review or decide before work continues.
practice_areas: Application engineering (product line); Business analysis; Disposal; Domain engineering; Integration and build; Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

theme: Requirements at every level and of every kind
definition: The level at which a requirement is stated: the organization's wish, the stakeholder's need, the system's obligation or an element's obligation; each level is derived from the one above.

theme: Requirements at every level and of every kind
definition: Turning a requirement at one level into requirements at the level below, repeatedly, as the structure of the solution becomes known; new stakeholders may appear at each step.

theme: Requirements at every level and of every kind
definition: Assigning a requirement to the part of the solution that will satisfy it, and noting what is left over.

theme: Requirements at every level and of every kind
definition: The sort of thing a requirement asks for, for instance what the product does, how well it does it, how it is used, how it connects to others, what it is made of or what it must protect; the kinds matter because each is checked differently.

theme: Requirements at every level and of every kind
definition: A requirement on what crosses the boundary between the solution and something outside it, or between two parts of it.
practice_areas: Business analysis; Integration and build; Technical (system) analysis

theme: Requirements at every level and of every kind
definition: A fact kept about a requirement besides its statement, such as its identity, owner, reason, source, priority, risk, state and how it will be verified.

theme: Requirements at every level and of every kind
definition: A property that a whole collection of requirements has or lacks, and that no single requirement can show, such as whether together they leave nothing out, contradict nothing and can be met.

theme: Requirements at every level and of every kind
definition: A rule for writing a requirement so that it is unambiguous, singular, measurable and testable, so that two readers cannot understand it differently.

theme: Requirements at every level and of every kind
definition: The decision, made when the requirement is written, of how it will later be shown to be met, by inspection, analysis, demonstration or test.
practice_areas: Business analysis; Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

theme: Requirements at every level and of every kind
definition: A quantity that tells whether the solution does the stakeholder's job (effectiveness) or how well the solution itself does what it does (performance).

theme: Requirements at every level and of every kind
definition: Counting what happens to requirements over time, such as volatility, coverage and progress, to steer the work.

theme: Operating context: how the product is meant to be used
definition: A description, from the point of view of the user and operator, of how the product is expected to be used, in what surroundings and by whom.

theme: Operating context: how the product is meant to be used
definition: A description of the organization's intended way of working with the solution, used to understand stakeholder intentions before they are formal requirements.

theme: Operating context: how the product is meant to be used
definition: A story of use stepping through who does what with the product to reach a goal, including the unhappy paths; it is both a source of requirements and a way to validate them.
practice_areas: Business analysis; Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

theme: Operating context: how the product is meant to be used
definition: A named goal that a user can achieve with the product, with the main way and the variations by which it is achieved.

theme: Operating context: how the product is meant to be used
definition: A distinct way the product is in use, such as normal, degraded, maintenance or training, each with its own behaviour and constraints.
practice_areas: Business analysis; Technical (system) analysis; Transition, deployment and release

theme: Operating context: how the product is meant to be used
definition: The line between the product and everything it deals with, and the description of what is on the other side.
practice_areas: Business analysis; Domain engineering; Technical (system) analysis

theme: Operating context: how the product is meant to be used
definition: The recognition that the product has different stakeholders and demands at different stages of its life, from idea to retirement.

theme: Shaping the solution: function and structure
definition: Breaking the required behaviour into smaller functions that together do the whole, so that each can be assigned, analysed and checked.

theme: Shaping the solution: function and structure
definition: How functions follow one another and which states the product passes through, described so that gaps and conflicts show up.

theme: Shaping the solution: function and structure
definition: A way in which a function can fail or be misused, found early by asking what could go wrong with each function.

theme: Shaping the solution: function and structure
definition: The arrangement of the solution by what its parts are for, independent of how they will be realized.

theme: Shaping the solution: function and structure
definition: The arrangement of the solution by what its parts are made of and where they run, derived from and traced to the logical structure.

theme: Shaping the solution: function and structure
definition: Studying safety, reliability, security or resilience as properties of the entire solution, since they cannot be read off any single part.

theme: Shaping the solution: function and structure
definition: Bringing the designs of different disciplines into one consistent solution, and preparing the later combination of their parts.
